chunks.title: Landmark Precedents in Indian Criminal Jurisprudence
chunks.content: # Landmark Precedents in Indian Criminal Jurisprudence

chunks.title: K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1962 SC 605
chunks.content:
### K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1962 SC 605
**Bench & Court:** Supreme Court of India (Subba Rao, J.)
**Core Holding:** Established the definitive test for "grave and sudden provocation" under Exception 1. The Court held that while a wife's confession of adultery constitutes grave provocation, the accused did not commit the fatal act in immediate reaction. Dropping his family at a cinema, driving to the naval dockyard, obtaining a revolver and cartridges under a false pretext, and proceeding to the victim's residence constituted a cooling-off interval with intermediate calculated steps that negated the element of suddenness as a matter of law.

chunks.title: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, (1984) 4 SCC 116
chunks.content:
### Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, (1984) 4 SCC 116
**Bench & Court:** Supreme Court of India (Fazal Ali, J.)
**Core Holding:** Formulated the five golden principles (Panchsheel) governing circumstantial evidence in criminal trials: (1) Circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is drawn must be fully established; (2) Facts must be consistent only with the hypothesis of guilt; (3) Circumstances must be of a conclusive nature; (4) They must exclude every possible hypothesis except the guilt of the accused; (5) The chain of evidence must be complete without leaving any reasonable ground for innocence.

chunks.title: Babu v. State of Kerala, (2010) 9 SCC 189
chunks.content:
### Babu v. State of Kerala, (2010) 9 SCC 189
**Bench & Court:** Supreme Court of India
**Core Holding:** Reaffirmed the bedrock principle that suspicion, however strong or grave, cannot take the place of legal proof beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution must establish an unbroken causal nexus between the accused and the alleged criminal act.

chunks.title: State of U.P. v. Deoman Upadhyaya, AIR 1960 SC 1125
chunks.content:
### State of U.P. v. Deoman Upadhyaya, AIR 1960 SC 1125
**Bench & Court:** Supreme Court of India
**Core Holding:** Clarified the admissibility of information leading to the discovery of a distinct physical fact under evidence law. The information must relate distinctly to the fact discovered in police custody to be admissible.

chunks.title: Akhtar v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2006) 10 SCC 473
chunks.content:
### Akhtar v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2006) 10 SCC 473
**Bench & Court:** Supreme Court of India
**Core Holding:** Re-emphasized that where an accused seeks the benefit of sudden provocation, the absence of prior premeditation and the immediacy of the retaliation are indispensable. Any conscious search for a lethal weapon after the provocation breaks the suddenness defense.

chunks.title: Procedural Practice Notes — Criminal Law & Trial Conduct
chunks.content: # Procedural Practice Notes — Criminal Law & Trial Conduct

chunks.title: Standard of Proof & Presumption of Innocence
chunks.content:
### Standard of Proof & Presumption of Innocence
1. **Unshifting Burden (BSA §104):** The prosecution bears the burden of establishing every material element of the charge beyond all reasonable doubt. The accused is clothed with a constitutional presumption of innocence until the final judicial holding.
2. **Standard on Exceptions (BSA §108):** When an accused invokes an affirmative defense (such as Exception 1 to BNS §103 for provocation or private defense), the standard of proof placed on the defense is preponderance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt.

chunks.title: Stage-Wise Examination Protocol under BNSS
chunks.content:
### Stage-Wise Examination Protocol under BNSS
1. **Examination-in-Chief:** Conducted by the party calling the witness to elicit material facts relevant to the indictment. No leading questions are permitted without the leave of the court.
2. **Cross-Examination:** Opposing counsel tests credibility, veracity, sensory vantage point, memory, and challenges inconsistencies with prior police statements. Leading questions are permitted.
3. **Re-Examination:** Confined strictly to explaining matters referred to in cross-examination; no new matters may be introduced without judicial permission.

chunks.title: Electronic Record Admissibility under BSA §61 / §63
chunks.content:
### Electronic Record Admissibility under BSA §61 / §63
For CCTV footage, call detail records (CDR), or computer logs:
- Must be accompanied by an electronic certificate identifying the device, verifying lawful control and uninterrupted integrity.
- Absence of a valid hash or chain of custody creates serious evidentiary gaps regarding tampering or spoliation.

chunks.title: BNS Section 103 — Murder
chunks.content:
### BNS Section 103 — Murder
(1) Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.
(2) Murder requires the causing of death with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause death, or if the act is done with the knowledge that it is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death.
(3) Statutory Elements: Actus Reus (causing death of human being), Mens Rea (intention to cause death or knowledge of imminent fatality), Absence of General or Special Exceptions.

chunks.title: BNS Section 103 Exception 1 — Grave and Sudden Provocation
chunks.content:
### BNS Section 103 Exception 1 — Grave and Sudden Provocation
(1) Culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, whilst deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation or causes the death of any other person by mistake or accident.
(2) Essential Provocation Rubric:
- Prong 1 (Gravity): The provocation must be grave enough to cause a reasonable person of ordinary temperament to lose self-control. Infidelity confessions or direct ocular discovery of adultery legally satisfy the gravity threshold.
- Prong 2 (Suddenness & Cooling-off Interval): The fatal act must be committed immediately upon the provocation before passion cools and self-possession returns. Any intermediate, calculated steps (traveling to a remote depot, procuring a firearm under false pretexts, deliberate transport between locations) legally demonstrate reflection and extinguish the suddenness element.
(3) First Proviso: The provocation must not be sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse for killing or doing harm.

chunks.title: BNS Section 303 — Theft
chunks.content:
### BNS Section 303 — Theft
(1) Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft.
(2) Statutory Elements: (a) Dishonest intention to permanently deprive (animus furandi); (b) Movable property; (c) Taking out of possession of another; (d) Absence of consent; (e) Physical moving of the property.
(3) Punishment: Imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

chunks.title: BNS Section 305 — Theft in Dwelling House or Custody Premises
chunks.content:
### BNS Section 305 — Theft in Dwelling House or Custody Premises
Whoever commits theft in any building, tent, vessel, office, or depository used as a human dwelling or for the custody of property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

chunks.title: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) Section 104 — Burden of Proof
chunks.content:
### Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) Section 104 — Burden of Proof
(1) Whoever desires any Court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist.
(2) In criminal prosecutions, the State carries the unshifting burden of establishing every statutory ingredient of the offence beyond reasonable doubt.

chunks.title: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) Section 108 — Burden of Proving Exceptions
chunks.content:
### Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) Section 108 — Burden of Proving Exceptions
When a person is accused of any offence, the burden of proving the existence of circumstances bringing the case within any of the General Exceptions in the BNS, or within any special exception or proviso, is upon him, and the Court shall presume the absence of such circumstances until established by the accused on a preponderance of probabilities.

chunks.title: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) Section 61 — Electronic Records
chunks.content:
### Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) Section 61 — Electronic Records
Electronic records are admissible as substantive evidence subject to certification verifying the device integrity, hash authenticity, and continuous chain of custody.
